dataset.name: NGEE Arctic Plant Traits: Nodule Biomass, Kougarok Road Mile Marker 64, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2017
description: Nodule biomass was measured within fifteen plots at the Kougarok hillslope site in June and July of 2017. The sampled plots were distributed across two ecotypes that contain the deciduous shrub Alnus viridis subsp. fruticosa (alder). Alder forms a symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria living within root nodules. Nodule biomass per unit area was determined with extensive soil core collection under the alder canopy. Alder height and basal area were also recorded. This dataset contains one csv file and one pdf file.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research.

The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska.

Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

measurementTechnique:
Soil core collection Plots were established and soil cores were collected from June 18th- July 28th, 2017. Destructive soil core collection similar to methodologies described in Ruess et al. (2013) and Uliassi & Ruess (2002). All cores were collected with a power drill with 7.3 cm diameter circular drill saw attachment. Cores were taken to a depth of 15 cm unless rock, coarse root, or standing water was encountered. The drill saw used for collecting soil cores was 5cm deep: when it was full the drill was pulled up and the soil was removed from the drill bit and placed in a plastic phototray before being bagged in a labeled ziploc. The length of the core was determined based on the depth of the hole left behind All sections of a core were bagged together and the total depth achieved for the core was noted. Within each nodule biomass plot, the basal area of all alder in the plot was measured at the soil surface using digital calipers. The maximum height of alder in the plot was measured to the nearest centimeter. GPS coordinates were marked with a handheld GPS unit (Garmin Montana 680t) or an iphone equipped with Avenza mapping application and a site-specific geoPDF. Sun and shade leaves were collected from alder in the plot (see Supplemental Files).
Alder is found within two ecotypes at Kougarok, Alder shrublands and Tussock tundra willow birch tundra. Within Alder shrublands, alder is the dominant species and forms a relatively closed canopy but in Tussock tundra willow birch tundra, alder grows with a mixture of other deciduous shrubs (Salix, Betula, and Vaccinium) and a graminoids. These two plant communities required different sampling techniques since alder is relatively homogenous in the Alder shrublands and heterogenous within the Tussock tundra willow birch tundra. In Alder shrublands, a 2.5 x 2.5m plot square plot was established. Within this plot, pin flags and meter tape were used to set up a grid containing 64 cells measuring 31 cm x 31cm. Letters were used to denote grid columns while letters were used to denote grid rows. Each grid cell therefore has a unique alphanumeric code and one soil core was collected per grid cell unless the cell was completely occupied by alder stem or rock. Grid cells where individual alders were rooted were recorded. To determine whether ramets of alder were part of the same individual, ramets were shaken and shallow coarse roots were traced. This plot type was called "square" and the sampling protocol described above resulted in destructive sampling of 3.9% of the total plot area. In Tussock tundra willow birch tundra, we selected an individual alder shrub and set up two concentric, circular plots with the alder at the center using pin flags.
The inner circle diameter was the alder's canopy and an outer circle was extended this boundary by 50 cm. The concentric circles were divided into eight equal slices, denoted by letters. We collected roughly twice as many cores from the inner circle as from the outer circle. Core placement (slice letter and inner versus outer circle) were recorded. This plot type was called "circular" and the sampling protocol described above resulted in destructive sampling of 3.4% of the total plot area. Following collection, all soil cores were place in coolers with blue ice for transport. Within twelve hours, the samples were transported to the lab in Nome and frozen. Frozen soil cores were then shipped to ORNL for processing.

Laboratory processing Soil cores were taken from freezer and thawed overnight. Each core was sorted for 10 minutes to remove any live root nodules present. Live nodule biomass was collected from each core, dead nodule biomass was not. Live nodules were differentiated from dead nodules based on their structural integrity and color. If the initial 10 mins of examination revealed signs of nodules (live or dead) the core was sorted for an additional 5 minutes to ensure that all live nodule biomass was found. Sorting time was extended another five minutes if more nodules were found. Sorting ended only when five minutes of searching yielded no nodules. Rocks over 2 mm in size were collected and rock volume was measured by water displacement within a graduated cylinder (0.1 cm3 accuracy). Following sorting, live nodules from each soil core were rinsed with DI and place in labeled coin envelopes. Nodules were dried in oven at 70 degrees Celsius for 48 hours and weighed after equilibrating to room temperature in a dessicator. 3. Data processing Nodule biomass per unit are and per unit soil volume were examined within square and circle plot types and no discernable spatial patterns were found. Within Alder shrublands, nodule biomass was not higher closer to alder stems. Within Tussock tundra willow birch tundra, samples collected within the inner circle did not have greater nodule biomass than samples from the outer circle. In Alder shrublands, nodule biomass per m2 ground area was calculated as the average nodule biomass per m2 across all replicate soil cores collected in the plot. In tussock tundra willow birch tundra, nodule biomass per m2 was first averaged across soil cores collected from the inner versus outer circles of the plot. These two values were a weighted-average nodule biomass per m2 for the whole plot. Weighting within this average was applied according to the area of inner versus outer circles. References Ruess, R.
